newsitem.title: USA: Panel recommends Perot be excluded from debates.
newsitem.headline: Panel recommends Perot be excluded from debates.

text.p: A commission planning for the 1996 presidential debates recommended on Tuesday that Reform Party candidate Ross Perot be excluded from debates between President Bill Clinton and Republican Bob Dole.

"The commission unanimously agreed with the unanimous recommendation of our independent advisory committee that only President Clinton and Senator Dole and their running mates be invited to participate," said commission co-chairmen Paul Kirk and Frank Fahrenkopf in a statement announcing the bipartisan panel's decision.
"Our decision ... was made on the basis that only President Clinton and Senator Dole have a realistic chance as set forth in our criteria to be elected the next president of the United States."
The panel said its decision to exclude Perot could be reconsidered for later debates -- three or four are in prospect -- if he improved his weak position in opinion polls.
The decision was a victory for Dole, who feared the participation of Perot in the widely-watched televised debates would siphon votes from him rather than Clinton.

Four years ago, when Perot played a prominent role in the debates and went on to win about 19 percent of the popular vote, many Republicans claimed he took votes away from then-President George Bush and helped elect Democrat Clinton.

The recommendation -- which would have to be accepted by the Clinton campaign to take effect -- brought an angry reaction from Perot's camp. His national coordinator, Russell Verney, called it "a travesty" and said the Reform Party was considering bringing suit in federal court against the commission.
At Perot headquarters in Dallas, angry Reform Party officials said they had not been notified in advance.

"They have not contacted us. They have only talked to the Republicans, the Democrats and the press," Perot spokeswoman Sharon Holman said. "It shows the extent to which they are trying to shut us out."
Dole representative, ex-South Carolina Governor Carroll Campbell, said the decision on Perot was the right one.

But the chief negotiator for the Clinton side in bargaining over debate terms, Commerce Secretary Mickey Kantor, told reporters at a news conference otherwise devoted to trade matters: "We regret that decision."
Kantor and Campbell planned to meet later on Tuesday to discuss the recommendation.

In 1992, Texas billionaire Perot ran as an independent candidate financing his own presidential campaign and took part in the debates. His third-placed presidential election finish was one of the strongest by a third-force challenger in U.S. history.

This year, he formed his own Reform Party and named maverick economist Pat Choate as his running mate. He qualified on the basis of his strong third-place showing in 1992 for $29.2 million in federal money to finance his 1996 run for the White House.
So far, however, Perot has garnered only single-digit support in opinion polls that place Clinton and Dole far ahead of him and Clinton well out front of Dole.

The Clinton and Dole campaigns have been meeting separately to discuss proposals for three or four presidential debates and one vice presidential contest. The first would tentatively take place either later in September or the first week of October. Election Day is November 5.

The commission was proposing ground rules for the debates -- which in the past have been subject to fierce bickering between the major candidates -- but its decisions are not binding unless accepted by those candidates.
The debates have become highlights of the presidential election seasons and a record 97 million Americans watched the final 1992 televised debate.
